size_note: market-wide; trillions in CHF positions built on the floor
pnl_note: EURCHF gapped far below 1.20 intraday; stops executed with extreme slippage
why_what: On 15 Jan 2015 the SNB discontinued the CHF 1.20 minimum exchange rate vs the euro without warning and cut its rate to -0.75%, saying the overvaluation had decreased while the euro was weakening globally.
how: Anyone long EURCHF at the floor was instantly offside as bids vanished; liquidity disappeared so stop losses filled far below trigger levels, producing losses larger than posted margin.
where_ctx: OTC spot, institutional and leveraged retail; announced Zurich morning, 15 Jan 2015.
lesson: Central bank floors are political decisions that can vanish overnight; gap risk overwhelms stop placement on one-way peg trades.

side: retail clients long EURCHF via FXCM
size_note: client negative equity balances of approximately $225 million owed to FXCM
pnl_note: FXCM said the debit balances risked breaching its regulatory capital requirements
why_what: The SNB floor removal caused unprecedented EUR/CHF volatility; FXCM's own SEC-filed release says clients experienced significant losses generating negative equity balances of about $225M.
how: Leveraged retail accounts went negative faster than margin close-out could act in a gapped market, transferring the loss to the broker; FXCM needed a $300M Leucadia rescue within a day.
where_ctx: US-listed retail FX broker; New York, 15 Jan 2015 press release filed with the SEC.
lesson: Broker counterparty solvency is part of trade risk; negative-balance protection did not exist yet for these accounts.

side: short CHF / long EURCHF-style macro bet
size_note: Everest Capital Global Fund, about $830M in assets at end-2014
pnl_note: lost almost all its money; fund closed
why_what: Everest's largest fund had been betting the Swiss franc would decline when the SNB scrapped the cap; Bloomberg reporting (via Reuters) cited a person familiar with the firm.
how: A leveraged short-CHF macro position was caught by a ~30% franc repricing in minutes; the position could not be unwound before the fund was effectively wiped out.
where_ctx: Miami-based hedge fund run by Marko Dimitrijevic; reported 17 Jan 2015.
lesson: Even professional macro funds die on peg breaks when leverage meets a discontinuous policy repricing.

size_note: open-ended SNB commitment to buy foreign currency in unlimited quantities
pnl_note: franc fell sharply from record strength after the announcement
why_what: On 6 Sep 2011 the SNB set a minimum exchange rate of CHF 1.20 per euro, calling the franc's value a threat to the Swiss economy, and committed to enforce it with unlimited FX purchases.
how: Traders who sold the franc alongside the central bank's credible unlimited commitment profited as EURCHF jumped off its lows; those fighting the floor lost for three years.
where_ctx: OTC spot; SNB press release, Zurich, 6 Sep 2011.
lesson: A central bank with unlimited balance sheet can dominate the exchange rate; align with credible commitments, fade them only when the politics crack (see forex-001).

side: short GBP vs the ERM band
size_note: UK spent billions of reserves and raised rates intraday defending the band
pnl_note: sterling left the ERM and devalued; the UK's defense cost billions
why_what: Sterling joined the ERM in 1990 and struggled to hold its band; on 16 Sep 1992 speculators attacked, the Bank of England's defense failed, and the UK quit the mechanism the same day.
how: Persistent selling of an overvalued pegged currency forced the defender to choose between economically ruinous rates and devaluation; the peg broke within a day.
where_ctx: London, ERM-era European FX; documented day-by-day in the Guardian's 20-year retrospective.
lesson: A peg inconsistent with domestic economics is a one-way bet: limited downside for attackers, unlimited cost for defenders.

size_note: massive leveraged short; widely reported around $10B with reported profit near $1B
pnl_note: reported profit about $1B (widely cited, not officially audited)
why_what: Soros judged Britain's ERM position unsustainable and that sterling would have to devalue or leave; he built the most prominent short among many speculators.
how: Quantum sold borrowed pounds for German marks and dollars, adding futures and options, so its own selling amplified downward pressure on the peg the BoE had to defend.
where_ctx: Macro hedge fund positioning into the 16 Sep 1992 break; mechanics summarized by Investopedia.
lesson: Reflexivity: a large enough actor's positioning helps cause the outcome it predicts; position sizing matched conviction.

size_note: sterling fell 18 US cents overnight; lowest since 1985
pnl_note: biggest one-day fall in living memory per Reuters
why_what: The UK voted to leave the EU on 23 Jun 2016 against market pricing; results through the night turned Remain optimism into a record sterling plunge, with the euro sliding 3.1% too.
how: Binary political event risk repriced a whole economy in hours; liquidity thinned through Asian hours and GBP longs had no orderly exit.
where_ctx: Global OTC FX through referendum night, 24 Jun 2016; Reuters market wrap.
lesson: Binary event outcomes cannot be hedged by conviction in polls; event risk demands flat books or optionality, not directional leverage.

side: any GBP exposure in early Asian session
size_note: 6.1% drop in about two minutes, then a partial snap back
pnl_note: stop cascades filled at extremes; mean-reversion buyers recovered much of it
why_what: On 7 Oct 2016 the pound plunged 6.1% in minutes during Asian hours, its biggest drop since the Brexit vote, with traders blaming computer-initiated sell orders (a fat finger or algos).
how: Thin liquidity plus algorithmic stop-triggering created a self-reinforcing air pocket; prices recovered quickly once human liquidity returned.
where_ctx: Early Asian session, thin liquidity window; Bloomberg market report.
lesson: Session liquidity is a risk factor: the same position is far riskier at illiquid hours; flash crashes punish tight stops and reward liquidity provision.

side: MoF long yen vs speculative shorts
size_note: record 6.35 trillion yen (about $48B) of dollar-selling intervention in Oct 2022
pnl_note: yen stabilized after interventions; officials said effects were 'certain'
why_what: USDJPY hit a 32-year low for the yen at 151.94 on 21 Oct 2022 as the BoJ held ultra-low rates while the Fed hiked; Japan's MoF confirmed record yen-buying intervention on 21 and 24 Oct.
how: Unsterilized dollar selling at psychologically loaded levels squeezed speculative yen shorts; disclosure of size reinforced the deterrent.
where_ctx: Tokyo; MOF quarterly disclosure reported by Reuters, confirmed Feb 2023.
lesson: Intervention works best when deployed against stretched one-way positioning at obvious levels; size disclosure is part of the weapon.

size_note: total intervention Apr-Jun 2024: 9,788.5 billion yen (official MOF disclosure)
pnl_note: temporary yen support; pair re-weakened until July policy shift
why_what: Japan's Ministry of Finance disclosed 9.79 trillion yen of FX intervention operations for April-June 2024, defending the yen at multi-decade extremes of dollar strength.
how: Repeated large dollar sales slowed but did not reverse the trend while the US-Japan rate gap persisted; the durable turn came only with BoJ tightening and US data shifts.
where_ctx: Tokyo; official MOF quarterly intervention operations page, published 7 Aug 2024.
lesson: Intervention can buy time and punish shorts, but cannot hold a level against an unchanged interest-rate differential.

size_note: dollar index to 102.68, weakest since Jan; Nikkei down nearly 20% over the move; bitcoin -15%
pnl_note: USDJPY fell 2.04% on the day to 143.5, a seven-month yen high
why_what: Weak US jobs data, disappointing big-tech earnings and China concerns sparked a global selloff and rate-cut bets; the yen surged as crowded carry positions unwound into 5 Aug 2024.
how: Short-yen carry trades (funding risk assets in near-zero yen) were forced to cover as the BoJ hiked and US recession fear rose, accelerating the yen's rise and global deleveraging.
where_ctx: Global macro deleveraging day, 5 Aug 2024; Reuters currency and cross-asset wraps.
lesson: Carry trades earn small steady differentials and lose them back in days when volatility regime-shifts; funding currency choice is risk selection.

size_note: described by the Fed paper as the most dramatic yen carry unwind on record
pnl_note: sharp yen appreciation in Oct 1998 inflicted large losses on carry positions
why_what: Immediately after the LTCM crisis, banks cut leverage to hedge fund clients; the Fed's IFDP 899 identifies October 1998 as the most dramatic episode of yen carry-trade unwinding.
how: Forced deleveraging after LTCM's collapse made funds buy back yen to close short-yen funding legs, compounding the yen's surge independent of Japan's fundamentals.
where_ctx: Post-LTCM global deleveraging; Federal Reserve International Finance Discussion Paper 899.
lesson: Carry unwinds are driven by lender margin calls, not just rate differentials; funding-side leverage is the hidden variable.

size_note: lira lost more than 34% vs USD since January 2018
pnl_note: record low 6.30 per dollar; Turkish equities -17%, bond yields ~18%, inflation 15%
why_what: The BBC's explainer records the lira nosediving through 2018 as investors lost confidence in Turkey's policy mix: political pressure for low rates, large dollar-denominated corporate debt, and a diplomatic rift with the US.
how: Foreign capital exited TRY assets faster than the central bank would defend with orthodox hikes, so the carry yield that attracted holders was swamped by depreciation.
where_ctx: Istanbul/EM FX; BBC explainer during the August 2018 trough.
lesson: High nominal yield is compensation for policy-credibility risk; when the central bank is not independent, carry is not a free lunch.

size_note: lira weakened persistently through 2021's rate-cut cycle
pnl_note: renewed record lows as unorthodox easing continued into high inflation
why_what: KBC's economic analysis describes Turkey 'testing the limits of unorthodoxy': repeated policy rate cuts under political pressure despite elevated inflation, eroding the lira through 2021.
how: Each cut lowered the real return on lira assets, prompting deposit dollarization and importer hedging that fed further depreciation in a loop.
where_ctx: EM FX research note, January 2022, covering the 2021 episode.
lesson: A currency's floor is set by policy credibility, not by how cheap it looks; negative real rates invite structural depreciation.

side: long RUB / short RUB defense by CBR
size_note: key rate hiked to 17% from 10.5% in one emergency move; 11.5pp of hikes in 2014
pnl_note: ruble staged its largest one-day fall since 1998 on 15 Dec
why_what: Falling oil prices and sanctions over the Ukraine crisis pushed Russia toward recession; on 16 Dec 2014 the central bank raised its key rate to 17% in an emergency move to halt the ruble's collapse.
how: Oil-linked revenue expectations collapsed with crude, and sanctions cut refinancing channels; even a 650bp overnight hike only partially stabilized the currency.
where_ctx: Moscow, overnight emergency decision reported by Reuters, 16 Dec 2014.
lesson: Commodity terms-of-trade shocks plus sanctions can overpower even extreme rate defenses; position sizing must assume policy arrives late.

size_note: record low 121.52 on 10 Mar; back past 72 by 8 Apr 2022
pnl_note: official rate round-tripped while everyday transaction rates diverged
why_what: After the invasion of Ukraine the ruble crashed to a record 121.52 per dollar on 10 Mar 2022, then staged an apparently extraordinary recovery that Reuters showed was not what it seemed: capital controls made the exchange rate artificial.
how: Mandatory export-revenue conversion, capital controls and frozen foreign sellers propped the official rate; the price used in everyday transactions was sometimes very different.
where_ctx: Moscow Exchange official rate vs controlled market reality; Reuters analysis, 8 Apr 2022.
lesson: Under capital controls the quoted FX rate is a policy artifact, not a tradable price; mark positions to the rate you can actually transact at.

side: short THB vs the dollar peg
size_note: peg defense drained Thai reserves before the float
pnl_note: baht devalued sharply; crisis spread to Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia
why_what: On 2 Jul 1997 Thailand abandoned its dollar peg after sustained speculative attack, triggering the Asian financial crisis; the Chicago Fed retrospective asks whether it was foreseen given the warning signs.
how: Attackers shorted an overvalued peg against dwindling reserves; once the float came, contagion repriced every similar peg and current-account deficit in the region.
where_ctx: Bangkok then regional contagion; Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Fed Letter No. 161 (Jan 2001).
lesson: Peg attacks are contagious: the same vulnerability map (fixed rate, weak reserves, external deficits) gets repriced everywhere at once.

side: global risk assets long China stability
size_note: yuan at four-year low after two days; global markets roiled
pnl_note: risk-off across equities and commodities on devaluation fear
why_what: On 11 Aug 2015 the PBoC revised how it calculates the daily guidance rate to better reflect market forces; the yuan fell sharply for two days to a four-year low, startling markets that read it as competitive devaluation.
how: A small technical fixing change was read as a policy signal of growth desperation; offshore-onshore spreads blew out and global risk assets sold off on imported-deflation fears.
where_ctx: Shanghai/offshore CNH; Reuters market report, 12 Aug 2015.
lesson: In managed regimes the signal value of a fix change matters more than its size; watch the fixing mechanism, not just the level.

size_note: sterling -3% to a 37-year low below $1.09; 5-yr gilts' biggest daily fall in 31 years
pnl_note: gilt-currency doom loop forced emergency BoE gilt purchases days later
why_what: Chancellor Kwarteng's mini-budget promised 45 billion pounds a year of permanent tax cuts plus energy support, requiring 72 billion pounds of extra borrowing in six months; investors choked on the prospect and hammered both gilts and sterling.
how: Fiscal credibility loss hit bonds and currency simultaneously, and leveraged LDI pension positions turned the gilt selloff into a forced-selling spiral that fed back into GBP.
where_ctx: London, 23 Sep 2022; Reuters market wrap.
lesson: In a twin-deficit country, fiscal credibility is the exchange rate; currency and bond risk are the same trade at stress points.

size_note: banking system near 1000% of GDP vs the state's rescue capacity
pnl_note: krona collapsed with the banks; capital controls imposed for years
why_what: The IMF's post-crisis interview explains Iceland allowed a banking system to grow from about 100% to close to 1000% of GDP after 2003 privatization, vastly outstripping the authorities' ability to act as lender of last resort.
how: When wholesale funding froze in 2008 the banks failed at once, taking the currency with them; no domestic backstop existed at that scale.
where_ctx: Reykjavik; IMF Survey interview, December 2008.
lesson: A currency is only as strong as the state's capacity to backstop its banking system; bank-sector size relative to GDP is an FX risk metric.

size_note: G5 finance ministers' coordinated statement
pnl_note: dollar entered a multi-year decline after the Plaza Accord
why_what: On 22 Sep 1985 the G5 ministers and governors announced agreement that further orderly appreciation of the main non-dollar currencies against the dollar was desirable, committing to coordinated intervention.
how: Simultaneous official signaling and intervention by five major economies repriced the overvalued dollar; positioning built on dollar strength was run over by policy coordination.
where_ctx: Plaza Hotel, New York; primary communiqué text via the University of Toronto G7 archive.
lesson: When major central banks coordinate against a currency, the policy signal itself is the trade; fighting coordinated intervention is fighting five balance sheets.

size_note: peso went from about 3.40 to 7.20 per dollar, recovering only to 5.80 after four months
pnl_note: Mexican prices rose about 24% in the aftermath; 'Tequila effect' hit Chile and Brazil
why_what: In December 1994 Mexico's crawling-peg defense failed amid political shocks and dollar-linked tesobono debt; the peso was devalued then floated, roughly halving in value before stabilizing.
how: Short-term dollar-linked government debt made the defense self-defeating: each devaluation increased the peso cost of tesobonos, accelerating reserve loss and the run.
where_ctx: Mexico City; crisis summary and figures from the Mexican peso crisis reference entry.
lesson: Currency mismatch on the sovereign's own balance sheet converts a defense into an accelerant; check what the defender owes before trusting the peg.

side: long BRL under the crawling peg
size_note: reserves peaked above $70B in early 1998 and roughly halved by year-end defending the real
pnl_note: January 1999 devaluation initiated what Dallas Fed called the first financial crisis of 1999
why_what: The Dallas Fed's retrospective explains Brazil's Real Plan peg/crawling band could not offset cumulative inflation differentials; contagion from Asia 1997 and Russia 1998 drove outflows that rate hikes and half the reserves could not stop.
how: Overvaluation plus fiscal stress plus external contagion drained reserves until the peg was abandoned in January 1999; the real then floated and depreciated sharply.
where_ctx: Brasilia; Dallas Fed Southwest Economy, March-April 1999.
lesson: Crawling pegs die by cumulative overvaluation, not by a single shock; reserve trajectory is the tell.

size_note: IMF approved a $50B stand-by arrangement, about 1110% of Argentina's quota
pnl_note: carry trade unwound into a run that forced the largest IMF program to that date
why_what: In 2018 a run on the peso driven by inflation, fiscal deficits and drought-hit exports forced Argentina to the IMF; on 20 Jun 2018 the Board approved a US$50B three-year stand-by arrangement.
how: High-yield local-currency paper attracted carry inflows that reversed when credibility cracked; the reversal size dwarfed the yield earned, a classic EM carry trap.
where_ctx: Buenos Aires/Washington; IMF press release 18/245.
lesson: When the carry trade on an EM currency ends at the IMF's door, the yield was the risk premium all along.

side: holders of pesos at the pre-devaluation official rate
size_note: 54% devaluation; official rate moved to 800 pesos per dollar, then a 2%/month crawling peg
pnl_note: purchasing power of official-rate peso balances more than halved overnight
why_what: On 12 Dec 2023 the Milei government devalued the peso by 54% as the first batch of shock measures, setting the official rate at 800 per dollar with a 2% monthly crawl, alongside subsidy cuts.
how: A deliberate administered devaluation transferred the adjustment to peso holders instantly; the gap between official and market rates was closed by decree, not by trading.
where_ctx: Buenos Aires; Bloomberg report on the shock package.
lesson: In administered regimes the overnight devaluation risk is the position; local-currency exposure carries full adjustment risk regardless of hedges priced off the official rate.

size_note: euro down 11.8% year-to-date at parity, first time below $1 in two decades
pnl_note: among the worst years in the euro's history per Reuters
why_what: On 13 Jul 2022 the euro broke parity with the dollar for the first time in twenty years as the energy price shock from the Ukraine conflict threatened a prolonged European economic crisis, while the Fed out-hiked the ECB.
how: Terms-of-trade shock: Europe's energy import bill exploded, flipping its current account, so the euro sold off on both growth fear and rate differential at once.
where_ctx: London/global FX; Reuters analysis at the parity break.
lesson: Terms-of-trade shocks can dominate rate differentials for commodity importers; the currency is where the energy bill shows up first.

size_note: reserves exhausted to the point of sovereign default
pnl_note: rupee devalued sharply in the 2022 balance-of-payments crisis
why_what: The IMF's 2023 staff report records that preexisting vulnerabilities, significant policy missteps (including late-2019 tax cuts costing over 2% of GDP in revenue) and major shocks produced Sri Lanka's full-blown 2022 crisis.
how: With reserves too low to defend any level, the rupee's managed rate broke, imports were rationed, and the sovereign defaulted; FX holders at the old parity absorbed the loss.
where_ctx: Colombo; IMF Staff Country Report 2023/116.
lesson: Reserve adequacy is the binding constraint on an EM currency; when reserves approach zero, the exchange rate is a countdown timer.

size_note: rand's biggest decline in more than four years
pnl_note: sharp one-day slump on a single political announcement
why_what: On 9 Dec 2015 President Zuma fired finance minister Nhlanhla Nene and replaced him with a little-known lawmaker, triggering the rand's biggest fall in over four years as fiscal-guardrail credibility was repriced instantly.
how: A single personnel decision destroyed the market's anchor for fiscal policy; no macro data changed, only the perceived guardian of the budget.
where_ctx: Johannesburg; Bloomberg report, December 2015.
lesson: In credibility-scarce markets, institutional personnel are a macro variable; political event risk can gap a currency without any economic release.

side: AUDJPY carry trade (long AUD, short JPY)
size_note: RBA cites evidence of very large carry unwinds in Aug 2007 and Oct 2008
pnl_note: negative FX return vastly outweighed the positive interest differential
why_what: The RBA's May 2009 Bulletin documents how carry trades in the Australian dollar unwound as the sharp AUD/JPY depreciation made positions unprofitable: the exchange-rate move swamped the small stable interest differential.
how: Falling AUDJPY forced liquidation, which pushed AUDJPY lower, forcing more liquidation, a self-reinforcing unwind that hit leveraged investors and Japanese retail margin traders alike.
where_ctx: Sydney/Tokyo flows; Reserve Bank of Australia Bulletin analysis.
lesson: Carry is short volatility: the exchange-rate leg, not the rate differential, decides the P&L in a crisis, and the unwind feeds itself.

side: short JPY in thin Asian-session liquidity
size_note: yen appreciated very sharply within minutes at the Asian open
pnl_note: stop cascades at extremes; prices and liquidity recovered quickly, no systemic effects
why_what: The RBA's Box B documents the 3 Jan 2019 flash event: the yen appreciated very sharply over a few minutes around the Asian open and cascaded across markets, with AUD depreciating sharply in low liquidity.
how: Holiday-thin liquidity, machine stop-triggering and retail margin dynamics concentrated in a few minutes produced an air pocket that mean-reverted once depth returned.
where_ctx: Asian session open, 3 Jan 2019; Reserve Bank of Australia Statement on Monetary Policy, Feb 2019.
lesson: Flash events cluster in predictable low-liquidity windows; avoid holding leveraged exposure through holiday Asian opens.

size_note: global dash for cash strained money market funds and FX swap funding
pnl_note: dollar surged on funding demand until Fed swap lines relieved the squeeze
why_what: The BIS Bulletin documents how Covid-19 stress in March 2020 produced turmoil in US dollar funding markets and money market funds: everyone demanded dollars at once, and the dollar spiked against nearly everything.
how: Non-US banks and corporates fund in dollars via FX swaps; when risk positions were liquidated, the funding legs had to be rolled or closed, converting a risk selloff into a dollar shortage.
where_ctx: Global dollar funding system; BIS Bulletin No 14, May 2020.
lesson: In a global crisis the dollar is a funding liability, not a currency view; the FX swap basis reveals funding stress before spot does.

size_note: euro opened at $1.17, close to estimated long-run equilibrium, then declined into 2000
pnl_note: multi-year slide from launch levels eventually drew coordinated intervention in Sep 2000
why_what: Randall Henning's study of euro-area intervention records that the euro opened at $1.17 on 4 Jan 1999, near economists' equilibrium estimates, yet slid through 1999-2000 amid strong-US growth expectations and cacophonous ECB communication.
how: A new currency with an untested central bank and conflicting official signals carried a credibility discount that persisted even with fundamentals near equilibrium.
where_ctx: Frankfurt/global FX; academic study 'Organizing Foreign Exchange Intervention in the Euro Area'.
lesson: Institutional credibility and message discipline are priced into a currency; 'fair value' is not a floor when governance is unproven.

size_note: EU-wide regulatory intervention covering all retail CFD and binary options providers
pnl_note: ESMA acted because a consistent majority of retail accounts lose money trading CFDs
why_what: On 27 Mar 2018 ESMA agreed to prohibit binary options to retail investors and restrict CFDs with leverage limits, per-account margin close-out, negative balance protection, a ban on incentives and standardized risk warnings.
how: The measures codify what broker disclosures show: leverage amplifies retail losses, so the regulator capped leverage and forced brokers to absorb negative balances rather than clients.
where_ctx: European Union; ESMA press release under MiFIR product-intervention powers.
lesson: Regulatory leverage caps exist because the structural edge in leveraged retail FX is against the client; treat any retail 'edge' claim with skepticism proportional to the leverage used.

side: retail follower of published trade ideas
size_note: self-reported $350 account, 1-2 trades per week
pnl_note: self-reported string of losing trades, including one taken without a stop loss; prior year claimed +21% (unverified)
why_what: A BabyPips member journaling their 2023 trading reports a run of losses while following a blog's chart trade ideas, admitting bad habits are catching up, including a trade with no stop loss.
how: Signal-following with small size and inconsistent risk control: skipped stops and late entries (6-8 hours after idea publication) degraded the edge the signal may have had.
where_ctx: BabyPips public trade journal thread, February 2023.
lesson: Self-reported retail results carry survivorship bias; even here the poster attributes losses to skipped stops, the classic failure mode, not to the strategy.

size_note: self-reported $1000 first live account
pnl_note: self-reported: burned through the first $1000 in about four months, avoiding a margin call only by stopping early
why_what: A BabyPips member's 'traders anonymous' confession describes blowing a first live account of $1000 over about four months, naming one culprit: not using a stop loss.
how: Undisciplined risk: trading without stops and splitting focus across methods drained the account steadily rather than in one blow.
where_ctx: BabyPips beginner forum thread, April 2009.
lesson: The canonical retail loss is slow bleeding without stops, not one dramatic trade; self-report, treat as anecdote not evidence of rates.
